::: research-question
## Research Question

**Does the vapor-phase enrichment process responsible for REE and beryllium mineralization at Round Top extend across the broader Sierra Blanca laccolith complex, or is it unique to Round Top itself?**

This research, conducted under Dr. Brent Elliott at the Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin, investigates the mineralogical and geochemical processes responsible for rare earth element (REE) and beryllium enrichment in the Sierra Blanca laccolith complex of far West Texas — one of the only known sources of heavy rare earth elements (HREE) currently under active commercial development in the United States bu US Rare Earths.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: site-overview
## Background

The Sierra Blanca Complex consists of five rhyolite laccoliths, Round Top, Little Round Top, Little Blanca, Triple Hill, and Sierra Blanca Peak, emplaced roughly 35–36 million years ago into Cretaceous sedimentary strata during a period of regional magmatism in the Trans-Pecos volcanic province. Round Top, the most thoroughly studied of the five, hosts an economically significant HREE deposit hosted primarily in the mineral yttrofluorite, alongside beryllium mineralization (bertrandite, behoite) and lithium enrichment in lithium-substituted mica.

This deposit is unusual among the world's major REE resources: most economic REE systems form in peralkaline or carbonatite settings, where alkali- or carbonate-rich melts and fluids readily mobilize REEs. Round Top is a peraluminous rhyolite — a melt chemistry that typically works against REE mobility. Exceptionally high fluorine content in the melt overcame this tendency, keeping REEs and associated elements (Be, Sn, Nb, Ta, Th, Li) mobile through late-stage magmatic crystallization and depositing them as a suite of disseminated, interstitial fluoride and oxide minerals through a process known as vapor-phase crystallization.

Subsequent geochronological work has added complexity to this story as some of the fluorite-bearing veins that crosscut the Round Top laccolith have been dated as tens of millions of years younger than the laccolith itself, indicating a distinct, much later hydrothermal remobilization event linked to Rio Grande rift-related fluid flow. Round Top's REE and critical mineral inventory therefore reflects at least two genetically and temporally distinct processes layered on top of one another: primary, syn-magmatic vapor-phase enrichment, and a younger structurally-controlled hydrothermal overprint.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: site-overview
## The Gap

While Round Top has been characterized in considerable mineralogical, geochemical, and geochronological detail, the same cannot be said for its neighboring laccoliths. Existing regional studies, whole-rock geochemical surveys and structural mapping across all five peaks, have established that the complex shares a common thermal history and that REE enrichment is present, to varying degrees, across the other laccoliths as well. Independent lines of evidence, including zircon trace-element chemistry and isotopic source studies, further suggest that the laccoliths are not petrogenetically identical, raising open questions about whether they share a common magmatic source and enrichment process, or represent distinct, if related, magmatic and hydrothermal histories.

Critically, no study to date has applied the mineral-scale petrographic and geochemical characterization needed to determine whether the same vapor-phase enrichment process and the same suite of REE- and critical-mineral-bearing phases are present at Little Round Top and Little Blanca specifically. Exploration data independently collected by industry partners has identified geochemical and mineralogical signatures at both peaks consistent with Round Top's known mineralization style, including a beryllium-conducive trace element signature at Little Blanca and physically exposed fluorite-behoite mineralization at Little Round Top, but these anomalies have never been examined at the mineral scale.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: site-overview
## Current Research

My thesis addresses this gap directly. Working in coordination with active exploration drilling at Little Blanca, I am conducting field sampling, petrographic analysis, and mineral-chemical characterization (XRF, SEM, and LA-ICP-MS) to determine whether these laccoliths host the same disseminated, vapor-phase REE-Be mineral assemblage documented at Round Top, a diminished expression of it, or a texturally and genetically distinct style of mineralization, including the possibility that structurally-controlled, younger hydrothermal processes, rather than primary vapor-phase crystallization, are responsible for what enrichment is present. Whole-rock geochemistry, including quantitative fluorine analysis, complements this mineral-scale work to place new petrographic observations in the context of the complex's existing geochemical dataset.

**Current status:** Seven representative samples from Little Blanca have been submitted for whole-rock geochemical analysis at [ALS Global](https://www.alsglobal.com) in Reno, Nevada, and for thin section preparation at [Quality Thin Sections](http://qualitythinsections.com) in Arizona. Petrographic and mineral-chemical analysis will follow once samples are returned.

This research sits at the intersection of igneous petrology and economic geology, with direct relevance to ongoing efforts to expand domestic critical mineral resources. Preliminary results are being presented at the Geological Society of America's GSA Connects 2026 meeting in Denver.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: site-overview
## Broader Significance

Beyond its immediate application to a single active mining prospect, this work speaks to a broader question in economic geology: whether unusually efficient critical mineral enrichment in evolved, fluorine-rich magmatic systems is a repeatable, predictable process, or the product of a rare and specific set of conditions unlikely to recur even within the same magmatic complex. Resolving this question at Sierra Blanca has direct implications for critical mineral exploration strategy across the broader Trans-Pecos magmatic province and in analogous fluorine-rich rhyolite systems elsewhere.
:::
